reading.title: Start with the question that the record can answer
reading.text: A comparison becomes useful when the reader can connect each number with a specific evaluation question. Before looking for the largest or smallest value, identify what was measured, what sample was used and which conditions were applied. A result may describe one observation without answering whether another formulation will behave the same way. Read the label, unit and note as a single statement. If any part is missing, keep the interpretation open rather than treating the record as a complete recommendation. reading.title: Keep the unit attached to the number
reading.text: A number without a unit leaves the reader to reconstruct an assumption that the source should have supplied. Density, surface area, percentage and elapsed time describe different properties, even when their values happen to look similar. A narrow screen should therefore preserve the unit beside the value or repeat it in an equally clear field label. The connection must remain clear after wrapping, opening a disclosure or moving to the next card. Do not infer a unit from the previous row, and do not rely on a desktop table heading that disappears in the mobile presentation.

reading.title: Read conditioning notes before drawing a comparison

reading.title: Record what is known and leave room for uncertainty
